extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and peer reviewers interested in peer review practice and reform
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for performing peer review, reporting peer-review processes, and assessing peer-review models (open peer review, preprints, editorial decision roles, transparency). Useful for reviewers, editors and scholars studying peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer status — Approved
rubrics_metrics.description: Approved — The paper is scientifically sound in its current form and only minor, if any, improvements are suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by reviewers to indicate the manuscript requires no major changes; implies suitability for publication/indexing as-is or with trivial edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer status — Approved with reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: Approved with reservations — A number of small changes, sometimes more significant revisions are required to address specific details and improve the paper's academic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates manuscript is potentially publishable but needs revision; reviewer should list specific required changes and their priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer status — Not approved
rubrics_metrics.description: Not approved — Fundamental flaws in the paper seriously undermine the findings and conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when essential methodological, conceptual, or ethical problems cannot be addressed by minor revision; reviewer should explain the fundamental flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods transparency and declaration of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should clearly state their methodological approach and limitations (for example, if the work is not a systematic review and no formal search strategy with keywords was undertaken).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly describe the methodology used, any search strategies, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and limitations so readers and reviewers can assess scope and strength of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic QC checks (ethics, trial registration, reporting guidelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review and journal QC should begin by checking for basics such as the presence of ethics statements, trial registration, and the use of reporting guidelines (e.g., EQUATOR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers/editors should verify required ethics declarations, trial registration numbers where applicable, and adherence to relevant reporting checklists as part of initial quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish summative (evaluative) vs formative (developmental) peer review roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review serves both summative roles (making acceptance/rejection decisions) and formative roles (providing feedback to improve authors' skills and manuscripts); these functions can be separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may choose to provide only developmental feedback (no explicit accept/reject recommendation) to encourage innovation, or provide evaluative judgements — clarify which approach is used and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer declaration of expertise and suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should state their expertise and attest that they have an appropriate level of expertise to judge the submission (e.g., 'I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a short statement of relevant qualifications/experience and any limits to expertise; this supports transparency and helps editors weigh reviewer comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing interests / affiliation disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and reviewers must declare competing interests and relevant affiliations (e.g., employment, funding, commercial relationships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, specific disclosures in the manuscript and review metadata (e.g., 'JPT works for ScienceOpen', institution paid APCs). Editors should ensure COI statements are visible and complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral, non‑emotive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid emotive or overly charged language in manuscripts and reviews (for example, avoid terms like 'gold standard' without qualification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise, measured phrasing; reviewers should flag emotive passages and suggest neutral rewording to improve objectivity and persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and avoidance of repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should avoid being overly long and repetitive; key topics should be consolidated to improve clarity and readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest structural consolidation where topics recur across sections; point out repeated material and recommend where to merge or remove redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and citation of reporting standards and professional bodies (EQUATOR, COPE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers discussing peer review or reporting research should reference and, where appropriate, adopt standards and guidance from organisations such as the EQUATOR Network and COPE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure correct attribution of roles (e.g., EQUATOR focuses on reporting guidelines) and cite/uphold current guidance for reporting and ethical issues in publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference hygiene and link permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: References should use recommended DOI formatting (https://doi.org/...), avoid outdated dx prefixes, and authors/journals should use web archiving tools (Wayback Machine, Perma.cc, WebCite) to prevent link rot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check DOI formatting, correct reference entries, and where web pages are cited, encourage archiving or including persistent identifiers to preserve the evidence base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and moderation of post-publication commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing post-publication commenting platforms (e.g., PubPeer, Reddit), acknowledge and manage problems associated with tone, anonymity, or pseudonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss risks of abusive or non-constructive comments, suggest moderation strategies, and consider how anonymity affects civility and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address interdisciplinary differences explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts about peer review should acknowledge and discuss complexity arising from interdisciplinary differences rather than treating peer review as uniform across fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit sections or caveats that explain how practices, norms, and expectations vary between disciplines and why that matters for proposed reforms or evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to copyediting: typos and sentence clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should identify typos, unclear sentences, and missing text, and request corrections (e.g., missing words, grammatical errors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag specific instances (with location) and suggest precise corrections; minor copyedits can materially improve comprehension and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency metadata for peer-review process (PRE example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review transparency can include metadata such as peer review method, number of rounds of review, number of reviewers and editors involved (example: PRE seal pop-up).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals/authors should include structured metadata reporting the review process to improve transparency and enable readers to verify how the paper was reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardise description of peer-review activities for recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardising how peer-review activities are described (not the activity itself) makes it easier to describe, attribute, recognise and reward reviewing work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt consistent vocabularies/metadata (e.g., Publons-style records, review badges) so that contributions are discoverable and creditable without forcing identical review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify roles: editors versus publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors manage editorial/review processes; publishers handle business processes — manuscripts and discussions should reflect this distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing peer review systems, be precise about which actor (editor, publisher, platform) is responsible for the practice or outcome under discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer and reviewer-type remuneration/recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that some reviewers (especially statistical reviewers) may be paid and that journals use incentives (free subscriptions, APC discounts) to reward reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider and report who is compensated and how; when proposing reforms, account for differing incentive structures (paid reviewers, waivers, recognition platforms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Label sections clearly (e.g., preprint repositories)
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing different publication infrastructures (e.g., digital repositories vs preprints), clearly label the section purpose (for example, explicitly state when a section refers to preprint repositories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguity by naming the category being discussed to prevent readers conflating distinct models or platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based assertions about harms (e.g., retaliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about harms or systemic problems (such as retaliation against reviewers) should be backed by documented evidence rather than asserted without substantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asserting risks like retaliation, cite studies or data; if evidence is limited, acknowledge uncertainty and avoid broad generalisations.
